report:
Historically, clinical evidence suggested a benefit. For example, a 2010 Cochrane review reported that probiotics reduced the mean duration of acute infectious diarrhea by approximately 25 hours (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532699/).

However, updated high-quality evidence has largely overturned this conclusion:

1. **2020 Cochrane Systematic Review Update:** A comprehensive update analyzing 82 trials found that when studies were restricted to those with a low risk of bias, probiotics showed little to no significant effect on reducing the overall duration of diarrhea or decreasing the likelihood of diarrhea lasting past 48 hours (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea; https://www.annemergmed.com/article/S0196-0644(21)00116-5/pdf).
2. **Clinical Practice Guidelines:** Reflecting these updated findings, the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) released 2020 guidelines recommending against probiotic use for acute infectious gastroenteritis in children due to a lack of high-quality trial evidence supporting its efficacy (https://medicalxpress.com/news/2020-06-aga-probiotics-digestive-conditions.html).

**Conclusion:**
Although earlier and lower-quality studies indicated that probiotics shorten acute infectious diarrhea, current high-quality scientific consensus indicates they do **not** meaningfully shorten the duration of the illness. Oral rehydration remains the primary standard of care.
